title: A planetary party portrait above Paranal
caption: Planets, the Moon and the Milky Way above Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Planets parade across the sky above ESO’s Paranal Observatory in this fish-eye view from early February 2025. Along with the Moon, the Milky Way and comet C/2024 G3 (ATLAS), the picture holds Saturn, Venus, Jupiter and Mars, and even Neptune and Uranus, too faint to pick out easily.

When several planets are up at once, you can often imagine a line through them. That is because the planets orbit the Sun in roughly the same flat plane, the ecliptic. In space they aren’t lined up at all, but now and then, every few years, many of them can be seen in the sky at the same time.

The planets sit outside the band of the Milky Way, and the line through them crosses it at an angle. The ecliptic is tilted by about 60 degrees to the plane of our galaxy: if the Milky Way were laid flat on a table, the Solar System would stick out like a pin poked in at an odd angle.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to B. Haeussler/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

alt: A round fish-eye view of the night sky over an observatory, with the Milky Way, the Moon and several bright planets strung across it.
